## Methods

Numerical simulations of light propagation in the non-Abelian topological insulator
We explain in detail how Fig. 3d, e is obtained from numerical simulations. We take Fig. 3e for example, in which we have considered a total of 205 samples with gout ranging between 0.2 μm and 4.5 μm, while all the samples share the same gin = 1.8 μm. In the simulation of each sample, we model the system by a Hamiltonian H(z) and solve the Schrödinger-like equation H(z)|φ(z)i = -i∂z|φ(z)i, where |φ(z)i is the state vector to be solved. To excite the edge mode II efficiently at the starting point, we choose |φ(z=0)i as the solved eigenvector of the edge mode II, which is given in the right panel of Fig. 3g. Since Fig. 3e only shows the field distributions in the lattice C, we only mark a star at site C2. The coordinates of the star, (1.8 μm, 2), mark the two key excitation parameters: gin = 1.8 μm and the site index n=2 corresponding to excitation site C2 on lattice C. After performing simulations for all the samples, we only extract the output result |φ(z=L)i for each case. By combining |φ(z=L)i of all the 205 simulations, we then draw |φ(z=L)i as functions of gout, which is finally shown in Fig. 3e. This is the procedure for obtaining Fig. 3d, e in numerical simulations. We introduce a detuning Δ to all the gap distances. The phase diagrams of two lattices, namely lattice I with Δ = -0.4 μm and lattice II with Δ = 0.4 μm, are shown on top of Fig. 4b, where the phase transition points are found to shift to a smaller (larger) g with a negative (positive) Δ. Such tunability allows us to combine the two lattices to demonstrate the non-Abelian bulk-boundary correspondence. Figure 4a shows the schematic diagram of a coupled system in which the light grey and dark grey waveguide arrays represent the defined lattices I and II, respectively. By setting the interface gap distance gb = 4.8 μm, we show the calculated eigenvalues of the system as a function of g in Fig. 4b, where the interface modes are marked by red. We calculate the associated non-Abelian topological charge of the combined system by using the non-Abelian quotient relation. The corresponding phase diagram is given on top of Fig. 4b, which is consistent with the distribution of all the interface modes. For example, in the defined phase region P2, the two interface modes are located in the second-third and fourth-fifth gaps, which resulted from the charge q123456 / q16 = q2345.

Sample fabrication and measurement
The photonic waveguide arrays were fabricated using the femtosecond laser direct writing techniques44–47. In our experiment, we focused a laser (Light Conversion CARBIDE 5W) inside a boroaluminosilicate glass chip (with a refractive index of ~1.504) by using a microscope with a numerical aperture of 0.75. To write photonic waveguides following a predesigned trajectory, the movement of the glass chip was controlled by using an Aerotech motion system with a moving speed of 40 mm/s. In the focused region of the laser, a refractive index increment of ~0.0025 can be induced, which then acts as the waveguide core, while the unaffected region acts as the waveguide cladding. The fabricated waveguide exhibits a cross-section of ~6 μm × 6 μm. In such a configuration, the waveguide supports only one vertical-polarized fundamental mode, which is used to probe the physics of the non-Abelian topological insulator. The length L of all the samples is 25 mm.

To effectively excite the topological edge mode and interface mode, we prepared a case-by-case excitation with a light field distribution similar to the eigenfield distribution of the desired mode. For the edge mode I in Fig. 3f, the light energy is mainly localized in waveguides A1 and C1, but the electric fields in the two waveguides are out of phase. To excite this anti-symmetric mode, we first used a Y-branch to split the injected laser into two beams. We then employed a three-waveguide system featuring a stimulated Raman adiabatic passage to generate a geometric phase π for one beam. Meanwhile, we applied another straight waveguide for transporting the other beam without this geometric phase. By connecting the two waveguides carrying these two beams with a phase difference π to waveguides A1 and C1, the edge mode I can be excited effectively. For the edge mode II in Fig. 3g, light is mainly localized in waveguides B2 and C2, while the corresponding electric fields in the two waveguides are in phase. By using a Y-branch beam splitter ahead of the sample, the edge mode II can be excited effectively. The edge mode III was excited using a similar method. For the interface modes I, II, and III, the distributions of light intensity and phase are even more complex, but our excitation method is still effective. Due to the difficulty in ideally exciting these interface modes, our experimental results are not exactly the same as the numerical results, but they still capture the key characteristic of the corresponding interface mode. At the output facet of the sample, we employed a charge-coupled device (XG500, XWJG) to collect the light intensity distributions.

At present, non-Abelian topological insulators have been verified in platforms such as metamaterials,
transmission line networks, and acoustic systems. However, in the field of photonics, which has rich
application potential, there is still a lack of feasible optical frequency implementation models. Moreover,
existing research mostly focuses on static systems with fixed topological charges, and the exploration of
dynamic phase transitions between different charges is insufficient. In addition, the traditional Zak phase
framework cannot accurately predict the distribution of edge states in multi-band systems. It is necessary to
solve the correlation problem between topological invariants and edge states in multi-band PT-symmetric
systems based on non-Abelian band topology theory.
In response to the above issues, this study proposes a minimum model of non-Abelian topological insulators.
A six-band non-Abelian topological insulator is experimentally achieved through a photonic waveguide
array at optical frequencies to explore dynamic non-Abelian topological phase transitions and verify the
domain wall state distribution dominated by non-Abelian quotient relations. At the same time, the model is
extended to a four-band system to prove its universality. However, I think the current version is not suitable
for acceptance by Nature Communications. Some modifications are necessary before acceptance.
We thank the reviewer for his/her efforts in reviewing our work and the positive remarks. The detailed
comments will be addressed below.

We first illustrate eigenvector rotation using a three-band example in Fig. R2. To explain the role of the
fundamental group in this context, it is helpful to use a real-space analog which is more intuitive. The
topology of defects in a biaxial liquid crystal can be described using exactly the same framework if we
associate a disclination (line defect) in the real space of a biaxial liquid crystal with a nodal-degeneracy line
in the band structure (momentum space) of a three-band periodic system with PT symmetry. In this mapping,
the orientation of the ellipsoidal liquid-crystal molecular frame in real space corresponds to the orientation
of the eigenvector frame formed by the three real eigenvectors of the k-dependent Hamiltonian in momentum
space. One can then consider a closed loop encircling a line defect: the orientation of the molecular frame
after going through one loop must come back to itself, and the rotation of along this loop provides a
topological classification of the enclosed disclination. By exact analogy, the rotation of the eigenvector frame
of 𝐻(𝐤)along a loop encircling a nodal line yields a topological classification of the nodal line itself.
The eigenvector frame of 𝐻(𝐤) can be represented by the principal axis of biaxial liquid crystal

7. The experiment observes the phase transition by changing the gap $g_{out}$ at the output end of the
sample. Essentially, it is a static comparative experiment rather than a real-time dynamic observation, which
cannot capture the evolution dynamics of the topological state during the phase transition process (such as
the time scale of edge mode disappearance), thus limiting the in-depth understanding of the non-Abelian
phase transition mechanism. This also goes against the authors' original intention, as in the introduction, the
authors explicitly mentioned the study of dynamical phase transitions.
Response:
We appreciate the comment by the reviewer. The reason we claim our system as a “dynamical” system is
that light propagating in the paraxial waveguides is governed by 𝐻(𝑧)|𝜑(𝑧)⟩=−𝑖𝜕 |𝜑(𝑧)⟩, where 𝐻(𝑧)
𝑧
and |𝜑(𝑧)⟩ are the Hamiltonian and state vector, respectively. The form of the master equation is in fact a
time-dependent Schrödinger-like equation in which the original time term t is replaced by a space dimension
term z. In our experiment, as the gap distance (which determines the topological charge) varies along the z
axis, light propagating in the system would experience multiple non-Abelian topological phases at different
“timeslots” 𝑧. Since different topological phases support different distributions of edge states, measuring the
existence of edge states in such systems would help us identify different topological phases and the phase
transition between them. This is motivation that we design such a system with varying structure parameters.
We agree with the reviewer that our experiment is a static comparative setup rather than a dynamic one.
Although the phase transitions can be probed in numerical simulations such as those in Fig. 3d,e, they cannot
be directly observed in experiments, since phase transitions only occur during the light evolution process,
while we can only measure the light distributions at the output side. Therefore, claiming that we have
observed the phase transition in experiment is not strict.
In the revised manuscript, we have removed all the statements associated with “dynamical phase
transition” in the Abstract, main text and Supplementary Information. Instead, we claim that the phase
transition can be probed in numerical simulations in the system with varying structural parameters, while in

## Paper

## Abstract

Non-Abelian topological insulators are multi-band systems, satisfying parity-time symmetry, characterized by fully gapped bands and whose topological charges are non-Abelian quaternions. These systems provide a richer landscape of edge and domain-wall states compared to that predicted by the Zak phase framework for Abelian topological insulators. Although non-Abelian topological insulators have been demonstrated in some proof-of-concept platforms, their realization in a photonic platform, where their characteristics are particularly valuable for on-chip applications, remains out of reach due to the lack of a feasible model. Here, we propose a minimal model for non-Abelian topological insulators and experimentally realize a six-band system at optical frequencies by using photonic waveguide arrays. A number of non-Abelian topological charges is experimentally demonstrated by probing the adiabatic evolution of edge states in a system with varying structural parameters. At the boundary between two samples with different non-Abelian topological charges, we experimentally observe domain-wall states that adhere to a non-Abelian quotient relation. The proposed idea can be generalized to an arbitrary number of bands and offer the flexibility to control multiple edge and domain-wall states in photonic devices.

---

## Introduction

Research on topological insulators has advanced significantly in recent decades1–5. The Zak phase is a key concept in topological insulators which represents the Wannier center’s displacement and relates to polarization, leading to charge accumulation at sample boundaries6–9. It can be used to predict edge states and is quantized to either 0 or π in parity-time (PT) symmetric systems. In conventional bulk-boundary theory, the Zak phase difference Δv across a boundary (either 0 or π) of a band gap predicts the number of boundary modes, given by Δv=π. However, this criterion is inadequate in multi-band systems where the number of bands n≥310,11. In this case, it is useful to use non-Abelian band topology theory12–42 to understand the relationship between topological invariants and edge states in multi-band PT-symmetric systems. Unlike conventional band theory that focuses on single band or band gaps, the non-Abelian band topology theory considers the eigenstates of all bands globally, drawing analogy of their eigenframe rotation in momentum space to the rotation of liquid crystal molecules around a loop encircling nematic liquid crystal disclinations, with topological charges represented by quaternions (n=3) or generalized quaternions (n>3). Here, PT symmetry constrains the Hamiltonian to remain real across the Brillouin zone, which facilitates topological characterization within a Clifford algebra framework. Currently, this theory has been applied in some multi-band systems, including those with band degeneracy and those with fully gapped bands. The former, known as non-Abelian semimetal, is primarily used to investigate trajectory-dependent nodal point collisions13,19, admissible nodal line configurations14,16,20–24, and the Euler class26–29,36,37. The latter, known as non-Abelian topological insulator, has unconventional bulk-boundary correspondence, which extends beyond the conventional description based on integers18,38. In contrast to conventional theories where domain-wall states are determined by the difference in topological charges, non-Abelian topology theory predicts them based on the quotient of charges which are matrix-like entities18. Up to now, non-Abelian band topological systems have been experimentally realized in various platforms including metamaterials17,20–22, transmission line networks18,38 and acoustic systems19,24,40. Advancing the field into technological areas, such as photonics, is of great importance, as the non-Abelian features and their associated matrix-form operations are useful for various applications, including optical computing and topological quantum computing. However, a model for realizing non-Abelian band topological systems at optical frequencies remains elusive, and corresponding experimental demonstrations have yet to be achieved.

In this study, we propose a minimal model for non-Abelian topological insulators with time-reversal symmetry and experimentally realize a six-band system at optical frequencies. We show that the non-Abelian topological charges in the six-band system describe eigenvector frame rotations as Bloch momentum changes and are characterized by generalized quaternions, including ±q123456, which have no counterparts in systems with n<6 and exhibit unique edge/domain-wall state distributions beyond the single-band Zak phase prediction. Subsequently, we experimentally realize the proposed model at optical frequencies in a laser-written photonic waveguide array. We design and implement an experimental configuration in which light could encounter structures with different non-Abelian topological phases along the propagation direction. In this way, different non-Abelian topological charges can be revealed in experiments. The non-Abelian quotient relation is also experimentally substantiated by constructing an interface between two samples with different non-Abelian topological charges.

---

## Results

Minimal non-Abelian topological insulator model with six bands
We first consider a quasi-1D tight-binding model as shown in Fig. 1a, which contains three coupled SSH chains. Each unit cell (dashed rectangle) contains six sites labeled “1” to “6”. The onsite energies and hopping strengths are chosen to ensure PT symmetry. The Hamiltonian is expressed as:

[Equation 1]

Here, h12 = w1 + v1 exp(-ik), h34 = w2 + v2 exp(-ik) and h56 = w3 + v3 exp(-ik), where k is the Bloch vector.

Before discussing the non-Abelian band topology, we first examine the correspondence between the single-band Zak phase and the existence of edge states. In Fig. 1b, c, we show the band structures (left panels) and energy spectra of finite samples with 20 unit cells (right panels) for two different parameter sets (see Supplementary Note 1). All the coupling strengths are set to be positive here. The Zak phases are labeled in the band structures. In the left panel of Fig. 1b, the Zak phases for the individual bands from first to sixth are all π, so if we sum up the Zak phases for the bands below a gap, the Zak phases for the first, third, and fifth gaps are π (dark gray), and the second and fourth gaps are 0 (light gray). According to the conventional bulk-boundary correspondence, the number of edge states in the first, third, and fifth gaps should be odd, while they should be zero in the second and fourth gaps. However, in the right panel of Fig. 1b, we find only three pairs of edge states in the third gap and none in the first and fifth gaps, which disagrees with the prediction from the Zak phase perspective. A similar analysis in Fig. 1c also shows deviations from conventional theory. Before explaining the failure of the Zak phase in predicting edge states, we first explain why this model can be considered a non-Abelian topological insulator.

According to the non-Abelian band topology theory, the PT-symmetric Hamiltonian H(k) can always be transformed into a real Hamiltonian He(k) through a unitary transformation He(k) = V*H(k)*Vy. The unitary matrix V can be derived from Takagi’s decomposition U = VVT, where U is a symmetric matrix representing the parity inversion operation. In our model, the unitary matrix V is chosen as [Equation 2].

After the unitary transformation, the obtained Hamiltonian is [Equation 3].

Here, he1 = w1 + v1 cos(k), he2 = w2 + v2 cos(k), he3 = w3 + v3 cos(k), he11 = v1 sin(k), he12 = v1 sin(k) and he33 = v2 sin(k). In this new Hamiltonian, all matrix elements are real, so the eigenvectors are real vectors denoted as u1, u2, u3, u4, u5, u6 T. These six real components define a 6D parameter space, and the evolution of the eigenvectors maps to trajectories within this parameter space as Bloch k varies. Considering all the band gaps between adjacent bands, the order-parameter space of the Hamiltonian is M = O(6)/O(1)6, where O(6) is the 6D orthogonal group and O(1)6 ≃ Z26 arises from the ±1 gauge freedom of the eigenvectors. The corresponding fundamental homotopy group is π1(M) = P6 ≃ Z25, which is formed by products of the ±1 gauge freedom, and the elements are [Equation 4].

The topological phase classification is determined by this non-Abelian fundamental group P6, and the group elements are referred to as the non-Abelian topological charges characterizing the topological phases. The group P6 has 64 elements grouped into 34 conjugacy classes: {+1}, {-1}, {±qij}, {±qijkl}, +q123456, and -q123456. The class {+1} denotes trivial rotation, and {-1} refers to a 2π rotation in any rotation plane. The ±qij represent ±π rotations in the rotation plane spanned by the eigenvectors of the i-th and j-th bands. The ±qijkl correspond to isoclinic double rotations of angle π in the 4D subspace of the i-th, j-th, k-th and l-th bands. The +q123456 and -q123456 correspond to triple rotations in the 6D space with opposite chirality. Figure 1d illustrates part of the group multiplication structure, showing elements as colored spheres and their multiplications with colored arrows. More group multiplication relationships are shown in Supplementary Tables 1-8.

Based on the above theoretical framework, the non-Abelian topological charges of the Hamiltonians in Fig. 1b, c are calculated to be q123456 and q1256, respectively (see Supplementary Note 2 for the calculation details). Their corresponding eigenvector trajectories within the u1u2u3, u3u4u6 and u4u5u6 subspaces are plotted in Fig. 1e, f, respectively, where the red, green, blue, purple, cyan, and yellow trajectories represent the tips of the eigenstates of the bands from first to sixth, with increasing line thickness showing k from -π to π. From Fig. 1e, all band eigenstates show a π rotation as the Hamiltonian evolves across 1D Brillouin zone, consistent with the charge q123456. In Fig. 1f, the first, second, fifth, and sixth bands rotate by π, while the third and fourth bands show trivial rotations, where their trajectory can be continuously contracted to a point, indicating a charge q1256.

Edge/domain-wall states of six-band non-Abelian topological insulators
We now discuss the edge states of the proposed six-band system and the inadequacy of the single-band Zak phase in predicting the existence of edge modes. Figure 1g shows the eigenvalue spectrum and the topological phase diagram obtained by varying a tunable parameter Δ = s = t in the minimal model of Fig. 1a. It displays the eigenvalue spectrum of a 20-unit-cell lattice, where edge and bulk states are distinguished by their inverse participation ratio (IPR). The IPR is defined as IPR = Σ|φi|4, where φi is the normalized wavefunction at lattice i. The states with a large IPR (appear in red) are considered edge states, while those with a small IPR (appearing gray) are considered bulk states. The corresponding IPR threshold is approximately 0.15. The diagram shows five phase regions separated by gap-closing critical points: P1 (q123456), P2 (q16), P3 (q123456), P4 (q1256), and P5 (q123456). The band dispersions shown in Fig. 1b, c correspond respectively to Δ = 0.5 and Δ = 2.5. To provide an intuitive understanding of this phase diagram, Fig. 1h illustrates a 2D parameter plane in momentum space, with each loop representing the Brillouin zone of a one-dimensional Hamiltonian. If the frame rotation of the 1D Hamiltonian along the loop is characterized by a specific generalized quaternion charge, then the loop encloses singularity points in the 2D plane, corresponding to gap-closing points of the Hamiltonian. A phase transition, marked by gap-closing of the Hamiltonian, occurs if the loop crosses these singularity points. We can label these singularity points with the generalized quaternion, indicating that loops that encircle those points are characterized by the same topological charges from a frame rotation perspective. Figure 1i shows representative field patterns of edge states, namely I and II, which are marked in Fig. 1g.

Since non-Abelian topological insulators need to consider multiple band gaps, the edge state distribution in the band structure becomes complicated. We first discuss the case of charges ±qij (i<j). In an ideal model with charge ±qij, where the rotational trivial bands are decoupled from the nontrivial (i-th and j-th) bands (with “nontrivial” referring to eigenvectors that rotate to their antipodal points in parameter space), and therefore the i-th and j-th bands form a two-band subsystem. The gap of this subsystem exhibits a Zak phase of π, while the trivial band has a Zak phase of zero. As a result, the system hosts an odd number of edge states. When perturbations couple the trivial and nontrivial bands, the charge ±qij can be factorized into a series product of charges, and all gaps between the i-th and j-th bands carry a Zak phase of π with an odd number of edge states. For instance, in the topological phase of q16 in Fig. 1g, each gap has one edge state, as q16 can be factorized into q16 = q12 q23 q34 q45 q56. Compared to the quaternion P3 in a three-band system corresponding to 3D rotation, the generalized quaternion P6 in a six-band system exhibits two kinds of unique topological charges: ±qijkl and ±q123456, which have no counterpart in P3. These charges correspond to double and triple rotations involving two and three orthogonal planes, respectively, thus cannot be described using the single band Zak phase description. The Zak phase of π only indicates the rotation angle of π but not the rotation plane, which becomes indeterminate in four or higher-dimensional spaces. Thus, while the Zak phase of π is useful in two-band and three-band systems, it does not provide sufficient information in higher-dimensional systems. Taking the charge q1256 as an example, it can be factorized in special cases into three forms: q12 q56, q16 q25, and -q15 q26. These factorizations can transform continuously without closing gaps, each representing a distinct combination of rotation planes and edge state distributions. In the general case, it is a superposition of these three factorizations and cannot be decomposed into the product of two simple topological charges. The edge state distribution also lies between these three factorization cases. For the charges ±qijkl, there are 15 distinct factorizations (C2C2=3!), leading to more complex edge state distributions. In the phase diagram of Fig. 1g, the edge states lie between various gaps depending on the factorization.

In non-Abelian band topology, the distribution of domain-wall states between two samples is related to the quotient of their topological charges, ΔQ = QL / QR, known as the quotient relation18. Here, QL and QR are the topological charges of the left and right samples. The distribution of domain-wall states is determined by ΔQ. Note that the quotient relation is valid only if the two samples share common gaps, allowing discussion of domain-wall states within the gaps in the original non-Abelian topological charge framework. We apply this principle to six-band non-Abelian topological insulators. In Fig. 2a, two samples with charges q123456 and q1256 are placed together, each with 20 unit cells. The couplings at the interface are averaged from the two samples (Fig. 2b). The Bloch bands for each sample are shown in Fig. 2c, and the energy spectrum in Fig. 2d reveals a single domain-wall state in the gap between the third and fourth bands, consistent with the quotient relation q123456 / q1256 = q34. Representative field patterns of edge and domain-wall states are shown in Fig. 2e. Similarly, for the q123456 and q16 samples (Fig. 2f–j), the energy spectrum (Fig. 2i) shows two domain-wall states in the second-third and fourth-fifth gaps, consistent with q123456 / q16 = q2345.

The quotient relation can be intuitively understood as follows. Similar to Fig. 1h, Fig. 2g displays a parameter plane, where each loop corresponds to a one-dimensional Hamiltonian. As we transition from the left domain q123456 to the right region q16 in real space across the boundary, this process can be represented in parameter space by contracting the loop from a bigger q123456 loop (solid yellow) to a smaller loop q16 (dashed yellow). The q123456 loop encloses charges q2345 and q16, while the q16 loop encloses only q16. As the loop contracts, it passes through q2345, causing the domain-wall state distribution to align with the edge state of this charge. It is important to note that the quotient relation has its own limitations. It is only capable of predicting the types of singularities that the closed loop will pass through, as well as the associated band gap closures, during the continuous transition between two Hamiltonians. Based on the Jackiw-Rebbi-type argument43, domain-wall states appear at gap-closing points, but this applies primarily to points near the gap closing. Therefore, if two samples, together with their domain wall, can be described by a parameter perturbation model around the phase transition point, the quotient relation can accurately predict the distribution of domain-wall states. However, when the parameter differences between the two samples are large, the distribution of domain-wall states becomes highly complex, making the quotient relation unable to directly predict their distribution. In our study, since the parameters of the two samples do not differ significantly, the prediction based on the quotient relation remains effective.

---

## Methods

Numerical simulations of light propagation in the non-Abelian topological insulator
We explain in detail how Fig. 3d, e is obtained from numerical simulations. We take Fig. 3e for example, in which we have considered a total of 205 samples with gout ranging between 0.2 μm and 4.5 μm, while all the samples share the same gin = 1.8 μm. In the simulation of each sample, we model the system by a Hamiltonian H(z) and solve the Schrödinger-like equation H(z)|φ(z)i = -i∂z|φ(z)i, where |φ(z)i is the state vector to be solved. To excite the edge mode II efficiently at the starting point, we choose |φ(z=0)i as the solved eigenvector of the edge mode II, which is given in the right panel of Fig. 3g. Since Fig. 3e only shows the field distributions in the lattice C, we only mark a star at site C2. The coordinates of the star, (1.8 μm, 2), mark the two key excitation parameters: gin = 1.8 μm and the site index n=2 corresponding to excitation site C2 on lattice C. After performing simulations for all the samples, we only extract the output result |φ(z=L)i for each case. By combining |φ(z=L)i of all the 205 simulations, we then draw |φ(z=L)i as functions of gout, which is finally shown in Fig. 3e. This is the procedure for obtaining Fig. 3d, e in numerical simulations. We introduce a detuning Δ to all the gap distances. The phase diagrams of two lattices, namely lattice I with Δ = -0.4 μm and lattice II with Δ = 0.4 μm, are shown on top of Fig. 4b, where the phase transition points are found to shift to a smaller (larger) g with a negative (positive) Δ. Such tunability allows us to combine the two lattices to demonstrate the non-Abelian bulk-boundary correspondence. Figure 4a shows the schematic diagram of a coupled system in which the light grey and dark grey waveguide arrays represent the defined lattices I and II, respectively. By setting the interface gap distance gb = 4.8 μm, we show the calculated eigenvalues of the system as a function of g in Fig. 4b, where the interface modes are marked by red. We calculate the associated non-Abelian topological charge of the combined system by using the non-Abelian quotient relation. The corresponding phase diagram is given on top of Fig. 4b, which is consistent with the distribution of all the interface modes. For example, in the defined phase region P2, the two interface modes are located in the second-third and fourth-fifth gaps, which resulted from the charge q123456 / q16 = q2345.

Sample fabrication and measurement
The photonic waveguide arrays were fabricated using the femtosecond laser direct writing techniques44–47. In our experiment, we focused a laser (Light Conversion CARBIDE 5W) inside a boroaluminosilicate glass chip (with a refractive index of ~1.504) by using a microscope with a numerical aperture of 0.75. To write photonic waveguides following a predesigned trajectory, the movement of the glass chip was controlled by using an Aerotech motion system with a moving speed of 40 mm/s. In the focused region of the laser, a refractive index increment of ~0.0025 can be induced, which then acts as the waveguide core, while the unaffected region acts as the waveguide cladding. The fabricated waveguide exhibits a cross-section of ~6 μm × 6 μm. In such a configuration, the waveguide supports only one vertical-polarized fundamental mode, which is used to probe the physics of the non-Abelian topological insulator. The length L of all the samples is 25 mm.

To effectively excite the topological edge mode and interface mode, we prepared a case-by-case excitation with a light field distribution similar to the eigenfield distribution of the desired mode. For the edge mode I in Fig. 3f, the light energy is mainly localized in waveguides A1 and C1, but the electric fields in the two waveguides are out of phase. To excite this anti-symmetric mode, we first used a Y-branch to split the injected laser into two beams. We then employed a three-waveguide system featuring a stimulated Raman adiabatic passage to generate a geometric phase π for one beam. Meanwhile, we applied another straight waveguide for transporting the other beam without this geometric phase. By connecting the two waveguides carrying these two beams with a phase difference π to waveguides A1 and C1, the edge mode I can be excited effectively. For the edge mode II in Fig. 3g, light is mainly localized in waveguides B2 and C2, while the corresponding electric fields in the two waveguides are in phase. By using a Y-branch beam splitter ahead of the sample, the edge mode II can be excited effectively. The edge mode III was excited using a similar method. For the interface modes I, II, and III, the distributions of light intensity and phase are even more complex, but our excitation method is still effective. Due to the difficulty in ideally exciting these interface modes, our experimental results are not exactly the same as the numerical results, but they still capture the key characteristic of the corresponding interface mode. At the output facet of the sample, we employed a charge-coupled device (XG500, XWJG) to collect the light intensity distributions.

networks, and acoustic systems. However, in the field of photonics, which has rich application potential, there is still a lack of
feasible optical frequency implementation models. Moreover, existing research mostly focuses on static systems with fixed
topological charges, and the exploration of dynamic phase transitions between different charges is insufficient. In addition,
the traditional Zak phase framework cannot accurately predict the distribution of edge states in multi-band systems. It is
necessary to solve the correlation problem between topological invariants and edge states in multi-band PT-symmetric
systems based on non-Abelian band topology theory.
In response to the above issues, this study proposes a minimum model of non-Abelian topological insulators. A six-band
non-Abelian topological insulator is experimentally achieved through a photonic waveguide array at optical frequencies to
explore dynamic non-Abelian topological phase transitions and verify the domain wall state distribution dominated by non-
Abelian quotient relations. At the same time, the model is extended to a four-band system to prove its universality. However,
I think the current version is not suitable for acceptance by Nature Communications. Some modifications are necessary
before acceptance.
My comments are:
1.Although the supplementary materials provide the multiplication table of Q_{64}, they do not elaborate on the numerical
calculation process of the generalized quaternion charge Q, such as the selection criteria for the number of discrete k points
and the numerical implementation method of the path ordered product. And how to map elements from $\mathfrak{spin}(N)$
Lie algebras to elements of generalized quaternion groups makes it difficult for readers to reproduce the calculation of
topological charges. It is suggested that the author take the four-band model as an example to illustrate how to obtain the
corresponding results.
2.The topological protection origin of non-Abelian topological charges was not explicitly expounded, such as its association
with system symmetries (PT symmetry, time-reversal symmetry).
3.What is the clear definition of the topological charge ?
4.What is the relationship between the elements of group Q64 and group Q16 and the topological edge states? How to
analyze this connection?
5.Although the supplementary materials present the research results of the four-band system, they do not systematically
compare the commonalities and differences between the four-band and six-band systems in terms of topological charge
classification, phase transition rules, and edge state characteristics, such as whether an increase in the number of bands will
introduce new topological phases, which fails to reflect the regularity of model expansion.
6.The article mentions the distinction between bulk states and edge states through the inverse participation ratio (IPR), but
does not provide a specific definition of IPR (nor does it explain the selection criteria for the IPR threshold), resulting in an
unclear basis for distinguishing marginal states from postures).
7.The experiment observes the phase transition by changing the gap $g_{out}$ at the output end of the sample. Essentially,
it is a static comparative experiment rather than a real-time dynamic observation, which cannot capture the evolution
dynamics of the topological state during the phase transition process (such as the time scale of edge mode disappearance),
thus limiting the in-depth understanding of the non-Abelian phase transition mechanism. This also goes against the authors'
original intention, as in the introduction, the authors explicitly mentioned the study of dynamical phase transitions.
8.What is the motivation for choosing s=t to conduct research? What changes will occur in the result if s is different from t?

The authors demonstrate the first photonic realization of non-Abelian topological insulators at optical
frequencies. They propose and carefully analyze a simple model supporting non-Abelian topological charges,
consisting essentially of coupled SSH chains. They realize the model using laser-written coupled waveguides,
and demonstrate both the delocalization of edge states across topological phase transitions along the
propagation direction, and the existence of interface modes between adjacent crystals with different
topological charge, a consequence of the non-Abelian bulk-boundary correspondence. The experimental data
look clean and are strongly supported by numerical calculations.

We first illustrate eigenvector rotation using a three-band example in Fig. R2. To explain the role of the
fundamental group in this context, it is helpful to use a real-space analog which is more intuitive. The
topology of defects in a biaxial liquid crystal can be described using exactly the same framework if we
associate a disclination (line defect) in the real space of a biaxial liquid crystal with a nodal-degeneracy line
in the band structure (momentum space) of a three-band periodic system with PT symmetry. In this mapping,
the orientation of the ellipsoidal liquid-crystal molecular frame in real space corresponds to the orientation
of the eigenvector frame formed by the three real eigenvectors of the k-dependent Hamiltonian in momentum
space. One can then consider a closed loop encircling a line defect: the orientation of the molecular frame
after going through one loop must come back to itself, and the rotation of along this loop provides a
topological classification of the enclosed disclination. By exact analogy, the rotation of the eigenvector frame
of 𝐻(𝐤)along a loop encircling a nodal line yields a topological classification of the nodal line itself.

7. The experiment observes the phase transition by changing the gap $g_{out}$ at the output end of the
sample. Essentially, it is a static comparative experiment rather than a real-time dynamic observation, which
cannot capture the evolution dynamics of the topological state during the phase transition process (such as
the time scale of edge mode disappearance), thus limiting the in-depth understanding of the non-Abelian
phase transition mechanism. This also goes against the authors' original intention, as in the introduction, the
authors explicitly mentioned the study of dynamical phase transitions.
Response:
We appreciate the comment by the reviewer. The reason we claim our system as a “dynamical” system is
that light propagating in the paraxial waveguides is governed by 𝐻(𝑧)|𝜑(𝑧)⟩=−𝑖𝜕 |𝜑(𝑧)⟩, where 𝐻(𝑧)
𝑧
and |𝜑(𝑧)⟩ are the Hamiltonian and state vector, respectively. The form of the master equation is in fact a
time-dependent Schrödinger-like equation in which the original time term t is replaced by a space dimension
term z. In our experiment, as the gap distance (which determines the topological charge) varies along the z
axis, light propagating in the system would experience multiple non-Abelian topological phases at different
“timeslots” 𝑧. Since different topological phases support different distributions of edge states, measuring the
existence of edge states in such systems would help us identify different topological phases and the phase
transition between them. This is motivation that we design such a system with varying structure parameters.
We agree with the reviewer that our experiment is a static comparative setup rather than a dynamic one.
Although the phase transitions can be probed in numerical simulations such as those in Fig. 3d,e, they cannot
be directly observed in experiments, since phase transitions only occur during the light evolution process,
while we can only measure the light distributions at the output side. Therefore, claiming that we have
observed the phase transition in experiment is not strict.
In the revised manuscript, we have removed all the statements associated with “dynamical phase
transition” in the Abstract, main text and Supplementary Information. Instead, we claim that the phase
transition can be probed in numerical simulations in the system with varying structural parameters, while in
experiment, we only identify different topological phases. We have rewritten all the corresponding contents.
Some key revisions are listed below for the reviewer to check.
Abstract: “Different non-Abelian topological charges have been experimentally demonstrated by probing
the adiabatic evolution of edge states in a system with varying structural parameters.”
Paragraph 2 in Introduction: “We design and implement an experimental configuration in which light
could encounter structures with different non-Abelian topological phases along the propagation direction.
In this way, different non-Abelian topological charges can be revealed in experiments.”
Paragraph 3 of the section “Experimental demonstration of edge states associated with different non-
Abelian topological charge”: “In experiments, the phase transition cannot be directly observed, as it occurs
during the light evolution process. Instead, this setting can be employed to distinguish different topological
phases, as crossing the phase transition point could affect the feature of the excited edge states.”
